newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian presidential candidate under the gun.
newsitem.headline: Colombian presidential candidate under the gun.

text.p: Colombia's most respected public figure is also one of the country's highest profile assassination targets, so much so that no one wants to have him as a neighbour.

But Alfonso Valdivieso, who resigned as the country's chief prosecutor last week, has a novel solution -- he hopes to move into Bogota's ornate Casa de Narino presidential palace in August 1998, if he can stay alive that long.

The man who would be president spoke of his ambitions, his housing problems, and some of the difficulties of public life in what he described as "the world's most violent country" in a Reuter interview late on Wednesday.
"I've had difficulty finding a home," Valdivieso, 47, said, sitting in the living room of his in-laws' apartment on the north end of the capital.
"There's a certain explicable sense of fear," he added, alluding to how no one wanted to sell a potential assassination victim a house because neighbours fear the threat of bombs going off next door.

"For the time being I've been living here," Valdivieso said of his in-laws' second-story apartment in an upmarket residential district. A dozen bodyguards guard the entrance, a closed-circuit camera offers sweeping views, and military police stand at barricades at both ends of the street.

Valdivieso was already considered a top potential target for assassination before he stepped down to run for the presidency. He said the security threat hanging over him since he was appointed prosecutor-general nearly three years ago had increased substantially since he announced his bid for the presidency.

His cousin Luis Carlos Galan, a charismatic and widely revered political leader, was cut down by an assassin's bullets while he ran for president in 1989. Valdivieso said only "maximum precautions" would prevent him from a similar fate.

"I know how difficult, torturous and particularly risky this is in our country," Valdivieso said of his fledgling campaign. "There's an unfortunate tradition of high risks in Colombia," he said, noting that he made many enemies as prosecutor.

The list is long. But in addition to spearheading an independent probe into drug-related financing of President Ernesto Samper's 1994 campaign, Valdivieso saw all of Colombia's billionaire cocaine merchants either killed or jailed on his watch as the country's top lawman.
He also locked up Samper's defence minister and attorney general and 10 other prominent politicians on narcotics-related corruption charges.

Valdivieso was constitutionally barred from prosecuting Samper, something he still clearly bridles at. The case he built against the president unleashed Colombia's worst political scandal in decades. But it was turned over to Congress, which ultimately exonerated Samper of all charges.

Polls consistently show Valdivieso to be Colombia's most admired public figure, a telling distinction for a crime fighter in a nation torn by seemingly uncontrolled levels of violence and the highest murder rate in Latin America.
But just as telling, perhaps, however popular he is, is the fact that no one wants to live next door to him.

The plucky Valdivieso stands barely five feet (1.52 metres) tall, but he said he intends to "measure up as a candidate" by offering strong "moral leadership" for a country whose woes include grinding poverty as well as criminal drug gangs and guerrillas.

He faces an uphill battle, since he plans to run as an independent and openly challenge Colombia's longstanding tradition of rule by the Liberal and Conservative parties. But Valdivieso is convinced that he has won broad-based support for his efforts to fight the drug-related corruption that has corroded virtually all walks of life in Colombia.
"I'm absolutely certain that I've contributed greatly to a growing awareness that organised crime represents a real threat," he said. "I think people will vote for that."
